info.title: LeadOcean API
info.summary: B2B people and company data — search, enrich and verify, over REST or MCP.
info.description:
B2B people and company data for software and for agents. Search a corpus of people and companies by filter,
enrich one person or one company into a full profile, and ask four narrow questions about a contact point —
over plain REST with an API key, or through the hosted MCP server with no key at all.

Everything below is generated from the running API, so it describes the service as it is right now.

## Base URL and authentication

```
https://api.leadocean.io
```

Send your key in the `x-api-key` header on every request. Keys carry scopes — `search` and `enrich` — and a key
without the scope an endpoint needs is answered `403` rather than an empty result, so a permissions mistake never
looks like a data gap. Create, view and rotate keys in your account.

```bash
curl -s "https://api.leadocean.io/v1/people/enrich?linkedin_url=https://www.linkedin.com/in/williamhgates" \
  -H "x-api-key: $LEADOCEAN_API_KEY"
```

## What a call costs

Usage is counted in **records**, never in requests. One person or one company returned is one record: a search page
of 25 rows costs 25, an enrichment costs 1 whether or not it finds anything, and each of the four contact endpoints
costs 1 for the same reason — they are doors onto the same lookup.

Sizing an audience is cheap and separate from pulling it: add `count=true` and the total comes back in `meta.total`,
capped at 100,000 — or withheld as `null` with `meta.totalWithheld` when a filter could not be applied, never published as a
number that does not mean what it looks like. A search row also publishes `has_email`, `email_status` and `email_type` as flags, so "does this
person have a deliverable address" is answered before you buy the address. Requests we reject are not counted.

## Rate limits, quotas and errors

Every response carries its own limits in headers: `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-Quota-State`, `X-Quota-Reset` and
`X-Quota-Contact`. A `429` means you went faster than your account’s per-second rate — wait for `Retry-After` and
retry. Running out of records does not cut you off on a paid plan: the API keeps answering at a reduced rate and says
so in `meta.notice` and `X-Quota-State` until the allowance resets.

Errors are a JSON envelope with `success: false` and a machine-readable `error.code`; the HTTP status and that code
always agree.

## What the email statuses mean

- **`verified`** — **we** sent to the address and the server accepted it. Not a claim inherited from a data supplier:
  a supplier’s word alone is published as `untested`, never as verified.
- **`catch_all_valid`** — a mailbox on a catch-all domain whose existence we confirmed through the provider's identity check (Microsoft 365 managed tenants and Google Workspace). Safe to send; ranks just under `verified`.
- **`catch_all`** — the domain accepts everything, so no per-address test can confirm or refute it. Labelled rather
  than quietly mixed in with the checked ones.
- **`untested`** — we hold the address and have not checked it ourselves.
- **`invalid`**, **`risky`**, **`disposable`**, **`role`** — checked and not safe to send to.

`verified_batch_date` is the date of the verification run that confirmed an address. A whole batch shares one date,
so read it as "checked in that run", not as a timestamp for that single address. `null` there means the verdict was
not ours — not that the address is bad.

## Naming a person

Any of `linkedin_url`, `email`, `phone` or `person_id` identifies a person. `person_id` is the one that always works:
about a fifth of the people search can find have no LinkedIn URL, and search publishes email flags rather than
addresses, so without the id that cohort would be findable and not enrichable. It is on every search row at
`meta.source_ids.person_id` and costs no more to use than any other key.

`person_id` names a **record**; `person_group_id` names the **person**. We hold more than one record for some people,
and which one a lookup lands on depends on the key you used, so the same human can come back under different
`person_id`s through different contact points. Two records sharing a `person_group_id` are the same person as far as
our de-duplication knows. Compare it; never look it up — `person_id` stays the key you send back.

## For agents

The hosted MCP server at `https://api.leadocean.io/mcp` gives Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, Codex and the rest the same surface as tools,
over OAuth 2.1 — your assistant signs in to your account and never handles a key. Set-up per client is in the guides.

## Guides and machine-readable copies

The long-form guides explain *why* you would call something and what the answers mean: [enrich a person](https://leadocean.io/docs/enrich),
[company lookup](https://leadocean.io/docs/company), [contact endpoints](https://leadocean.io/docs/contact), [search](https://leadocean.io/docs/search),
[filter reference](https://leadocean.io/docs/filters), [records, limits and errors](https://leadocean.io/docs/limits) and [MCP for agents](https://leadocean.io/docs/mcp).

The same surface in three machine-readable forms: [openapi.json](https://api.leadocean.io/openapi.json) for code generation,
[llms.txt](https://api.leadocean.io/llms.txt) for a short index an agent can read, and [llms-full.txt](https://api.leadocean.io/llms-full.txt) for the
exhaustive field-by-field description. All three are generated from the running API and cannot drift from it.

get.description: Filters combine with AND; multiple values inside one filter combine with OR. Each person returned counts one record. Page with meta.nextCursor. One search pages through at most 10,000 rows by default; past that no further cursor is issued and meta.depthCapped is true. The figure is per account — support can raise it for a genuine large export, so ask rather than working around it. It counts rows paged through and is not the monthly records allowance, which is separate. The answer to a capped walk is to narrow the filters and run several smaller searches; paging harder returns no more cursors. A walk of the WHOLE result set is order=stable: id order, on the snapshot the first page read (a 410 means that snapshot was retired mid-walk — start again without a cursor); an account enabled for unlimited walks pages it to its end, up to 200 rows a page, while every other account keeps the depth above and 100 rows.

parameters.name: order
parameters.description: ranked (default): best matches first. stable: every match in id order (person_id / company_id), unscored, on the index snapshot the first page read — for walking a whole result set. Pass order=stable with every page: a stable cursor only continues a stable walk, and a ranked cursor only a ranked search. If the snapshot is retired mid-walk the next page answers 410; start the walk again without a cursor. An account enabled for unlimited walks pages a stable walk to its end, with no depth cap, up to 200 rows a page; everyone else keeps the normal depth and 100 rows.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: Also return the exact total number of matches in meta.total. On the PEOPLE search it is opt-in because it is work: a page is ranked either way, a total has to be tallied. The COMPANY search counts its first page regardless and carries the figure in the cursor, so every page of a company walk has meta.total without recounting. FREE WITH limit=1: that combination is a sizing call, costs no records however often you send it, and answers with an empty `data` and `meta.countOnly: true` — the number is the answer, and a count that handed back its row would be a page of one record for nothing. With any larger limit you are buying the page as usual and the total rides along with it. Accepted on the JSON body form too. If a requested filter could not be applied (see unsupportedFilters), the total is withheld — null, with meta.totalWithheld saying which filter — rather than published as a number that does not mean what it looks like.

email_type.description: Kind of the person's best email address. work is at their CURRENT employer's domain. work_other is a business address at a different company — usually a former employer, so it is the one most likely to bounce or to reach whoever inherited the mailbox; ask for it deliberately, not by accident. work_any is the union of the two. personal is webmail and similar; other is a business address where we do not know the employer; unknown means the address exists but we cannot classify it, which is the most common answer; none means the person has no email. email_status.description: Deliverability of the person's best email, from verification rather than a guess. On a BUSINESS address (`work`, `work_other`, `other`), `verified` means OUR OWN verifier sent to the address and it accepted — nothing else earns the word, and a data supplier asserting that an address is good is not a check, whichever supplier it is: those are published as `untested`. PERSONAL ADDRESSES ARE THE EXCEPTION and the difference is worth knowing: we do not verify consumer domains at all, so on a personal address `verified` still means a supplier asserted it and you should treat it as a lead to verify rather than a confirmed one. The dedicated personal-email endpoint publishes no status for that reason. `catch_all` means WE probed the domain, on the same rule and with the same personal-address exception. In practice that changes nothing for catch_all — a catch-all verdict can only come from probing the domain, which no supplier does — so the whole of the current catch_all population already qualifies. This narrowed on 2026-09-20 and again on 2026-09-22, so a `verified` count taken before either date is not comparable with one taken after — the population is smaller each time and every address in it has been tested by us. ONE INCONSISTENCY WHILE THIS ROLLS OUT: enrichment (/v1/people/enrich, the v2 contact endpoints, MCP) applies the narrow rule per address; people search does not, because the search index carries no per-address verification provenance. A person can come back `verified` in a search row and `untested` when enriched, and the enriched answer is the correct one. Treat a search count of `verified` as an upper bound and confirm per address on enrichment. Safe to send: verified, and catch_all_valid — a mailbox on a catch-all domain whose EXISTENCE we confirmed through the provider's identity check (Microsoft 365 managed tenants and Google Workspace only; the domain would accept any address, this one is known to be real). It ranks between verified and catch_all and is earned only by that check, never by a supplier and never by re-reading an older catch_all verdict. As a FILTER, `catch_all` matches both catch_all and catch_all_valid (a confirmed mailbox is still on a catch-all domain), so an existing verified+catch_all filter keeps the promoted people; filter on `catch_all_valid` alone for the narrow set. Cannot be confirmed either way, because the domain accepts everything: catch_all. Do not send: invalid, spam_trap, abuse, disposable. Use with care: risky, role (a shared mailbox like info@) and derived (built from the company's address pattern and never tested). untested means nobody has checked this address yet — it may well be fine, and it is the largest group; unknown means it WAS checked and the result was inconclusive, which is a weaker signal than untested, not a stronger one. none means the person has no email.

'99' is the source's "unclassified" marker, kept by decision (2026-10-03) so companies and people carrying it can be filtered and counted.

FilterContract.description: What GET /v1/filters and its two narrower forms answer with. The narrow forms carry `scope` and one filter set; GET /v1/filters carries both sets under `filters` and `companyFilters`, plus an inline enum index.

filters.description: Filter name to { type, enum, desc, max, default }. On the scoped endpoints this is that scope’s set.

enums.description: GET /v1/filters only — the enum index, values inlined for the small sets.

schema.description: The record schema name this scope returns.

total.description: How many values the enum has.

matched.description: How many matched q — which can exceed the number returned, because values is capped by limit.

labels.description: Human labels, for the enums that have them.

filters.description: A people search filter set — every /v1/people/search filter except cursor, limit, count and facets

limit.description: Rows to export; at most the per-export ceiling (50,000)

columns.description: Column ids from /v1/exports/columns, in order. Omit to use a preset; the default preset is `full`.

preset.description: A named column set. `full` (default, 45 columns): identity, profile, address, contact flags, emails 1–3, phones 1–2, current role, education, skills — needs the enrich scope. `search` (27 columns): only what the search row carries, no contact points. Every row costs one record whatever the columns.

caps.description: Numbered-block sizes 1–10: emails (3), phones (2), past (3), educations (2), certifications (2), awards (1)

reveal.description: Derived from the columns when omitted

downloadUrl.description: Present once there is a file. A signed link that opens without an API key (the same kind the ready email carries), minted on every read, valid until downloadExpiresAt.

downloadNote.description: The same in words, for a person or an agent to relay: how long the link works without a key, that reading the export again gives a new one free (nothing is rebuilt), and until when the file is kept.

rows.description: Rows written so far, deduplicated by person_id

released.description: Reserved records given back when the export ended

pollAfter.description: Seconds to wait before polling again; null when finished

remaining.description: On creation only: records left after this reservation (null = unlimited plan)

perRow.description: On creation only: records per row (1, or 2 with an enrichment)

Fill.description: How many of the people in this row carry each contact point. A person is counted once per column however many addresses they hold.

anyEmail.description: Hold at least one email address of any kind

work.description: Hold at least one business address — at the current employer (work) or a former one (work_other); the emailType=work_any filter

personal.description: Hold at least one personal address

phone.description: Hold at least one phone number

regions.description: NORAM, EMEA, APAC, LATAM, Other — in that order, always all five. Region people sum to total.

code.description: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2; null for people with no country, under Other

PaceWindow.description: One fair-use window: how many records of this kind the account may receive in it, how many it has, and when it resets.

window.description: h5 = rolling 5-hour block, d = UTC day, w = week from Monday 00:00 UTC, p = the billing period

Account.description: One document per account. `records.ceiling` is null on a fair-use plan (nothing to run out of); `records.whenOver` says what happens past it: throttled (paid, paced to 1 request a minute) or refused (free plan, 402). `pace` is the fair-use pace of the 2026-10 plans (Solo, Agency, Platform): the windows the account is bound by, separately for search and enrichment, and which one is slowing it right now, if any. `subscription` is null until the account has ever subscribed.

key.description: The calling key; null for a signed-in session.

pace.description: null on a plan without a pace (Free, and the older paid plans with a monthly records figure). Reaching a window never refuses: calls of that kind are served at 1 request a minute until it resets, the other kind at full speed, and every answer carries X-Quota-State: paced, X-Quota-Reset and a meta.notice with code fair_use_paced. Calls that cost no records are never paced.

company.description: Present only on an account whose company-search records are paced apart (kind company: company5h, companyDay, companyWeek, companyMonth). Everywhere else company searches count as search.

paced.description: The window pacing the account now, with its kind; null at full speed.

search.description: What a people search returns on this account and how deep searches page. view thin = role, function, seniority, location and person_id, plus the parts thinFields lists (first_name; company = the employer block) — null thinFields is the default thin row, which carries the employer. companyMaxDepth is the people maxDepth unless set. deepWalk names the searches this account may walk to their END on order=stable (no depth cap, up to 200 rows a page). companyPace true = company-search records count under the pace kind company, not search. paceNotice true = the account is emailed once when a monthly pace window reaches 80%.

Usage.description: Your own account. Counted over the PLAN’s period, which is not always a calendar month — read `period` and `resetsAt` rather than assuming.

month.description: The counter bucket this period is keyed by.

period.description: month, billing period, or lifetime for a one-off allowance.

monthlyCredits.description: null on a fair-use plan — there is no number to run out of.

daily.description: The last 30 days, one row per day per key.

perKey.description: The same 30 days totalled per key.

Quota.description: The account's records are spent. On Free that is permanent: the 1,000 are a one-off allowance and do not reset. A paid account is paced to 1 request/minute instead of refused, until its billing date.

RateLimit.description: Over a key's own limit (key_rate: its requests a second; key_quota: its search rows or enrichments for today or this period, Retry-After = seconds to the reset and X-Key-Limit-Reset its time), or over the account rate — the plan's requests a second (Free 5, Solo 50, Agency 200, Platform 10,000), or 1 a minute while a fair-use window is reached (code fair_use_paced, with kind, window, windowLimit, windowUsed and resetsAt in details; X-Quota-State: paced) or while an older paid plan is past its monthly records (X-Quota-State: over-limit) — honour Retry-After
